language_wrapper: In a math contest, the committee fixes an exponent {exponent_a}. Determine the minimal positive integer n ≥ {lower_bound} for which there exists a bijection f: {1, ..., n} → {1, ..., n} satisfying both of the following for all x, y in {1, ..., n}: (i) If n divides {exponent_a}·x − y, then n+1 divides f(x)^{ {exponent_a} } − f(y). (ii) If n divides x + y, then n+1 divides f(x)·f(y) − 1. Find n.
hardness_rationale: This family strengthens the original AIME seed by imposing two simultaneous conjugacy constraints: a multiplicative-dynamics condition (edges defined by y ≡ a·x mod n must map to exponentiation by a modulo n+1) and an additive-to-multiplicative duality (edges defined by y ≡ −x mod n must map to multiplicative inversion modulo n+1). Solving requires recognizing a discrete-logarithm-style bijection f(x) = g^x onto the cyclic group modulo n+1 (with g a primitive root), and showing that it simultaneously linearizes both relations. This demands group-theoretic insight (primitive roots, cyclic groups, exponentiation homomorphisms), factorization of n+1−1, and a structural conjugacy argument rather than mere modular arithmetic. The verifier enforces the difficulty by explicitly finding a primitive root and checking all induced edges, preventing trivial guessing.
notes: Key insight: For prime p = n+1 with primitive root g, the map f(x) = g^x sends addition and scalar multiplication in the exponent (mod n = p−1) to multiplication and power operations in Z_p^×. Thus both constraints hold: y ≡ a·x (mod n) ↔ g^y ≡ (g^x)^a (mod p), and y ≡ −x (mod n) ↔ g^y ≡ (g^x)^{-1} (mod p). Minimal n is the least n ≥ lower_bound with n+1 prime. Verifier confirms by constructing g and testing all edges from these two relations.
source_question: Find the minimal positive integer \(n \geqslant 866\) satisfying: there exists a bijection \(f\) from \(\{1,\cdots,n\}\) to itself, such that for any \(x,y\in\{1,\cdots,n\}\), if \(n\) divides \(866x - y\) then \((n + 1)\mid f(x)^{866} - f(y)\).
